summary: For ages 7-9 (Lower KS2 / Grades 2-4): the insect body plan. Adult insects have three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen), exactly six legs that all attach to the thorax, usually one pair of antennae on the head, and a hard outer exoskeleton instead of internal bones. Most adult insects also have wings. The load-bearing facts are the count (six legs, three parts) and the location (legs attach to the thorax). This becomes the main rule children use to recognise an adult insect (young stages such as caterpillars or maggots can look different).
misconceptions: 'Spiders are insects' — spiders have 8 legs and 2 body parts; the six-legs/three-parts rule excludes them.
'Insects have bones' — they have an exoskeleton, not an internal skeleton.
'Legs come from all over the body' — all six attach to the thorax specifically.
'All insects have wings / anything with wings is an insect' — wings are common but not defining.
'Any small crawly thing is an insect' — the term is precise, not a synonym for 'bug' or 'minibeast'.

activities.title: Label and count on a real insect
steps: Look closely at a real specimen or a large, clear photo of a beetle or bee.
Point to and label the three body parts: head (front), thorax (middle), abdomen (back).
Count the legs one by one, 1 through 6, and trace each leg back to where it joins the body.
State out loud: 'Six legs, and they all attach to the thorax — the middle part.'
Find and name the antennae on the head; point to where the wings attach (the thorax).
activities.insight: An insect has three body parts and exactly six legs, and all six legs (and the wings) attach to the thorax specifically — not the head or abdomen.

activities.title: Bones inside or shell outside?
steps: Feel an arm or leg and notice the hard bone is on the INSIDE of the body.
Look at a beetle shell or a shed exoskeleton (or a close-up photo) and notice the hard part is on the OUTSIDE.
Compare a human x-ray picture (skeleton inside) with the beetle's armour (skeleton outside).
Say in your own words: 'An exoskeleton is a skeleton on the outside — a hard shell that holds the insect's shape and protects it.'
Answer: if an insect has no bones inside, what holds its shape? (Its exoskeleton.)
activities.insight: Support and protection can come from a hard covering on the OUTSIDE (exoskeleton), not only from bones on the inside; insects use an exoskeleton instead of an internal skeleton.

activities.title: Build a valid insect / apply the rule
steps: Assemble a model insect from parts: one head, one thorax, one abdomen, joined front-to-back.
Attach exactly six legs — all to the thorax (middle part).
Check your build against the rule: three parts, six legs, legs on the thorax.
Test whether other creatures fit the rule: a spider has 8 legs and 2 body parts, with legs coming off the front part — is it built the same way? (No — not an insect.)
Explain your decision: 'It has six legs and three parts, legs on the thorax, so it is an insect' — or why something is not.
activities.insight: The body plan works as a recognition rule: an adult insect has three parts and six legs attached to the thorax, so a creature that breaks the rule, like a spider with 8 legs and 2 body parts, is not an insect.

checkQuestion: Here is a picture of a beetle. Point to its head, its thorax, and its abdomen, and tell me how many legs it has and where they attach. Then tell me: does a beetle have bones inside like we do, or something else — and why does it need that?
checkAnswer: The beetle has three body parts: head (at the front, with the antennae), thorax (the middle), and abdomen (the back). It has exactly six legs, and they all attach to the thorax (the middle part), never to the head or abdomen. A beetle has no bones inside — it has an exoskeleton, a hard outer shell on the outside, which protects and supports its body.
